paragraphs: Answering many numerical questions privately usually means adding noise to the collection of answers. The central design choice is how to distribute that noise so that it protects the data while keeping answers useful. This paper studies that trade-off when the answer vector has many dimensions, seeking sharper conclusions than bounds that agree only up to constant factors.

The authors prove a central-limit-type result: under specified conditions on the noise, the resulting mechanism is approximately Gaussian differentially private. This describes the mechanism’s privacy behavior, rather than requiring the added noise itself to be Gaussian. The conditions cover a family of noise densities defined using powers of standard p-norms.

Using this perspective and the Cramer–Rao inequality, the paper derives a lower bound linking the privacy parameter, squared-Euclidean-style error, and dimension. Within the noise class covered by the analysis, Gaussian noise achieves the optimal privacy–accuracy trade-off with sharp constants. Numerical experiments support these theoretical findings. The scope of the optimality claim is the analyzed noise family.
neurips-2021-a-central-limit-theorem-for.tldr: A high-dimensional privacy theorem establishes sharp optimality of Gaussian noise within a specified class of private query-answering mechanisms.

paragraphs: An agent that cooperates successfully with its training partners may still struggle with a human whose habits and abilities differ. Training against a model of human behavior can help, but building that model first requires collecting human demonstrations. This paper investigates whether useful human collaboration can instead emerge from training entirely with artificial partners.

The proposed method, Fictitious Co-Play, trains an agent to respond effectively to a population of self-play agents. Crucially, that population includes saved versions from different stages of those agents’ training. These past checkpoints broaden the range of partners encountered during learning. The approach puts diversity of training partners at the center of preparation for unfamiliar collaborators.

Experiments use a two-player collaborative cooking simulator. In that setting, Fictitious Co-Play scores significantly higher with unfamiliar artificial and human partners than self-play, population play, and training against behaviorally cloned human models. Human participants also report a strong preference for the resulting partners. These findings support partner diversity as an effective route to human collaboration in the studied environment.
neurips-2021-collaborating-with-humans-w.tldr: Training against diverse self-play agents and their past checkpoints produces effective human collaborators without human training data in a cooking simulator.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model may generate fluent text without satisfying all the attributes a user wants. Fine-tuning offers one way to control those attributes, but it can demand substantial computation and suitable training examples. This paper introduces MuCoCO, an algorithm that applies control during generation using a pretrained model.

MuCoCO treats decoding—the process of choosing the output text—as an optimization problem. Desired attributes enter that problem as differentiable constraints, allowing several requirements to be represented together. Because text choices are discrete, the method first relaxes the problem into a continuous form. It then uses gradient-based optimization and Lagrange multipliers to incorporate the constraints into the search.

This formulation makes the control mechanism modular: different differentiable requirements can be incorporated into the same decoding framework. The authors evaluate the approach on machine translation and style transfer with multiple sentence-level attributes, reporting significant improvements over the tested baselines. The stated results support continuous constrained optimization as a practical approach to controlling several aspects of generated text at inference time.
neurips-2021-controlled-text-generation-.tldr: MuCoCO controls multiple text attributes by treating generation from pretrained models as continuous optimization with differentiable constraints.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among examples to extend a small set of known labels to unlabeled data. Its working assumption is that similar examples are likely to have similar labels. Yet the graph that encodes similarity is itself a consequential design choice, often determined through heuristics or domain-specific judgment.

This paper proposes learning that graph construction from previous problem instances in the same domain. Rather than fixing graph hyperparameters by hand, the approach learns settings within commonly used parametric graph families. It also accommodates combinations of substantially different similarity measures and the learning of multiple hyperparameters.

The authors provide formal guarantees in two settings. For online learning, they develop efficient algorithms with low regret; for distributional learning, they establish generalization guarantees. These results connect performance on available problem instances to performance on new instances from the same domain. The contribution is a principled way to learn a component that strongly influences label inference, while retaining the graph-based methods’ reliance on similarity as useful evidence about labels.
neurips-2021-data-driven-semi-supervised.tldr: The paper learns graph-construction hyperparameters from related problem instances and proves online and distributional guarantees for semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: An iterative learning algorithm can access training data repeatedly while releasing only its final model. When its intermediate states remain private, estimating leakage by adding up privacy costs for every computation can overstate what the released model reveals. This paper studies how privacy loss actually evolves during noisy gradient descent.

The analysis follows the distributions of model parameters produced from neighboring datasets, which differ in the data relevant to the privacy comparison. It tracks their Rényi divergence and establishes a provably tight bound on that quantity. This gives a dynamic account of privacy throughout training rather than only a cumulative accounting of intermediate operations.

For smooth, strongly convex losses, the authors prove that privacy loss approaches its limit exponentially quickly. This improves on composition-based bounds in the setting where internal states are private. With the additional Lipschitz condition, they also prove optimal utility using a small number of gradient computations. The results tie both privacy behavior and learning quality to explicit assumptions on the loss functions.
neurips-2021-differential-privacy-dynami.tldr: A tight analysis of noisy gradient descent shows exponentially converging privacy loss under smoothness and strong convexity when intermediate states remain private.

paragraphs: Neural optimal transport solvers can perform well inside applications, but that does not directly show whether they solve the transport problem accurately. This paper develops a quantitative benchmark for transport with quadratic cost, the setting associated with the Wasserstein-2 distance. The central obstacle is obtaining known correct transport maps between continuous distributions.

The authors use input-convex neural networks to construct pairs of distributions whose optimal transport maps can be calculated analytically. This makes it possible to compare a solver’s output against an actual reference solution. The construction also supports high-dimensional continuous distributions, including distributions in image spaces.

Evaluating existing solvers reveals that many fail to recover the correct transport maps faithfully despite useful downstream performance. Further experiments in image generation examine this mismatch and show that greater transport accuracy does not necessarily correspond to better application results. The benchmark therefore separates two questions that can otherwise be conflated: whether a method solves optimal transport accurately and whether it produces useful results in a downstream task.
neurips-2021-do-neural-optimal-transport.tldr: Analytically solvable transport benchmarks reveal that downstream success can coexist with inaccurate neural optimal transport maps.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization problems can contain variables that do not contribute to the final solution. Safe screening identifies such variables early, allowing the optimization process to exclude them with a mathematical justification. This paper develops a framework for making those decisions and applies it to least-squares problems with norm regularization.

The framework is built on Fenchel–Rockafellar duality, which provides a complementary mathematical view of an optimization problem. From this framework, the authors derive a screening rule called dynamic Sasvi. The rule generalizes an earlier method while removing its requirement for the exact solution of a more strongly regularized problem.

That change matters because the screening decision no longer depends on having that separate exact solution available. The authors state that the resulting rule operates safely in practice and always eliminates more features than the existing state-of-the-art methods they compare against. The contribution concerns the strength of certified feature elimination: it increases how much of the problem can be screened out while preserving the safety of those decisions.
neurips-2021-dynamic-sasvi-strong-safe-s.tldr: Dynamic Sasvi strengthens safe feature screening for norm-regularized least squares without requiring an exact solution to a more strongly regularized problem.

paragraphs: Routing decisions become harder when network costs fluctuate because of disturbances or changing traffic. This paper studies adaptive learning in nonatomic congestion games, a framework for congestion involving individually negligible participants. Its focus is reaching equilibrium efficiently both when network conditions are fixed and when they are stochastic.

Standard exponential weights achieves an equilibrium convergence rate of order 1/sqrt(T), but this leaves potential speed unused in static networks. Accelerated alternatives reach order 1/T² in the static case, yet the abstract reports that they fail to converge in stochastic problems. The proposed AdaWeight method adapts between these two regimes within one exponential-weights approach.

AdaWeight guarantees the faster rate for static environments and the stochastic rate under uncertainty, without requiring prior knowledge of problem parameters or optimizer tuning. The analysis also gives a subquadratic dependence of convergence speed on network size. Together, these results address both environmental uncertainty and scaling, supporting a single adaptive routing method across the two studied operating conditions.
neurips-2021-fast-routing-under-uncertai.tldr: AdaWeight adapts automatically between accelerated equilibrium convergence in static networks and robust convergence in stochastic congestion games.

paragraphs: High-resolution images contain useful detail, but processing the entire image becomes increasingly expensive as resolution grows. Traversal Network, or TNet, addresses this by selectively examining informative regions at multiple scales. It traverses the image’s scale hierarchy from the top down, using hard attention to choose which locations receive processing.

The number of attended locations provides an adjustable balance between accuracy and computational cost. TNet is also modular: most image classification models could supply its feature-extraction backbone. This means the proposed selective traversal can be combined with benefits from existing optimized classification architectures. Its chosen regions additionally provide a degree of interpretability without an extra inference procedure.

On ImageNet, TNet achieves higher accuracy than the tested hard-attention baselines while using fewer operations, less processing time, and less memory. On fMoW satellite images up to 896 by 896 pixels, it achieves higher accuracy and up to 2.5 times faster processing than baselines using the same resolution. These results support selective access to detail as a useful strategy for scaling image classification.
neurips-2021-hard-attention-for-scalable.tldr: TNet selectively visits informative image regions across scales to improve classification accuracy while reducing computation on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks with discrete choices or combinatorial solvers creates a training challenge: ordinary gradient methods do not pass straightforwardly through discrete computations. Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or I-MLE, provides a framework for learning such combined models end to end. Its scope includes discrete exponential-family distributions alongside differentiable neural components.

The framework requires the ability to find the most probable discrete states and does not depend on replacing the problem with a smooth relaxation. It encompasses perturbation-based implicit differentiation and approaches for differentiating through black-box combinatorial solvers. The authors also introduce noise distributions for approximating marginal probabilities by perturbing a problem and finding its most probable state.

In some previously studied learning settings involving combinatorial solvers, the authors show that I-MLE reduces to ordinary maximum likelihood estimation. Experiments across several datasets suggest performance that is competitive with, and often better than, methods using problem-specific relaxations. The contribution is both a shared perspective on existing techniques and a broadly applicable route to training models with discrete internal computations.
neurips-2021-implicit-mle-backpropagatin.tldr: I-MLE enables end-to-end learning through discrete distributions and combinatorial solvers using most-probable-state computations without smooth relaxations.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates clients through a central server while allowing them to train locally. Clients can differ in their objectives and computing capabilities, and communication may be infrequent or compressed. The paper identifies a speed–accuracy conflict in various existing methods: some converge quickly to the wrong point, while others reach the global minimum only at a slower rate.

The proposed FedLin framework addresses these challenges together. When each client’s loss is smooth and strongly convex, the authors prove linear convergence to the global minimum despite arbitrary objective and systems heterogeneity. The guarantee therefore combines rapid convergence with the correct optimization target under the stated loss assumptions.

The analysis also gives matching upper and lower convergence bounds that expose the effect of periodic, infrequent communication. For sparse gradient communication, FedLin retains linear convergence even with aggressive sparsification, and the authors quantify how compression changes the rate. These results explain how communication choices affect optimization speed while establishing conditions under which client differences do not force a loss of final accuracy.
neurips-2021-linear-convergence-in-feder.tldr: FedLin guarantees linear convergence to the global minimum for smooth, strongly convex client losses while addressing heterogeneity and sparse communication.

paragraphs: One alternative to training a neural network by backpropagation is to treat every unit as a reinforcement learning agent. The network then becomes a team whose members learn through local rules influenced by a shared global signal. The paper studies this approach as a form of learning more consistent with observed synaptic plasticity.

Training all units with REINFORCE follows the return gradient in expectation, but its high variance makes learning slow. MAP propagation is introduced to reduce that variance substantially while preserving the local character of the learning rule. It therefore targets the practical obstacle that has made teams of learning units difficult to use in deep networks.

In experiments using an actor–critic network, MAP propagation solves common reinforcement learning tasks at a speed similar to backpropagation. This finding supports the feasibility of the team-of-agents approach for the tested tasks. The result concerns learning speed and retained locality; the biological motivation comes from the structure of the learning rule rather than a claim that the method fully reproduces biological learning.
neurips-2021-map-propagation-algorithm-f.tldr: MAP propagation reduces variance in locally trained teams of neural units, reaching learning speeds similar to backpropagation on tested reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization searches using function evaluations rather than direct access to gradients. It is useful in settings such as query-based black-box adversarial attacks and reinforcement learning. Prior information can guide gradient estimates built from finite differences, but promising empirical behavior alone does not explain whether those guided methods converge.

This paper analyzes prior-guided optimization within a greedy descent framework, considering several gradient estimators. A central result is a convergence guarantee for prior-guided random gradient-free algorithms. The analysis gives a theoretical basis for incorporating prior information into the estimation process, addressing a gap between existing practical results and understanding of the algorithms’ behavior.

The authors also introduce an accelerated random search algorithm that incorporates prior information, together with its own convergence analysis. This extends the investigation beyond greedy descent toward faster search. Experiments on numerical benchmarks and adversarial attacks support the theoretical results. The contribution combines analysis of existing prior-guided methods with a new accelerated method, linking the use of prior knowledge to formally studied optimization progress.
neurips-2021-on-the-convergence-of-prior.tldr: The paper proves convergence results for prior-guided zeroth-order optimization and introduces an analyzed accelerated random search method.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to prepare a model to adapt to new tasks, often through an optimization process nested inside another training process. This paper instead trains a network end to end with persistent memory distributed across its layers. Changes in that memory carry the full responsibility for guiding adaptation to a task.

The placement of memory throughout the network is central to the approach. Ablation experiments show that supplying relevant feedback to memory units at different depths enables them to coordinate adaptation across the whole network. The result is a way to train adaptation behavior through a standard end-to-end procedure rather than casting it as a bi-level optimization problem.

The authors report performance exceeding gradient-based, prototype-based, and other memory-based meta-learning strategies. The approach also handles online situations in which a sample is observed substantially before its label arrives, a setting where the compared approaches struggle. Results span classification through online few-shot semantic segmentation, supporting distributed memory as a useful mechanism for adaptation across the studied learning tasks.
neurips-2021-online-meta-learning-via-le.tldr: Memory distributed across network layers supports task adaptation through ordinary end-to-end training, including online learning with delayed labels.

paragraphs: A selective classifier can either predict a label or abstain, potentially requesting more expensive processing. This paper studies an online setting where the true label becomes available only after abstention. Data need not be perfectly classifiable, so abstaining can remain a sensible long-term decision rather than merely an initial learning phase.

The goal is to make few mistakes while avoiding too many additional abstentions. The comparison is with the best classifier in a given class that, in hindsight, makes no errors and abstains as little as possible. This benchmark recognizes that even the reference classifier may need to decline some predictions.

The authors construct versioning-based algorithms with a tunable trade-off. For a parameter μ between zero and one, they bound mistakes by T^μ and excess abstentions by roughly T^(1−μ), suppressing logarithmic factors, even against adaptive adversaries. They also show that this dependence on the time horizon is tight. Experiments on realistic datasets illustrate the trade-off between making predictions and obtaining the feedback needed to learn.
neurips-2021-online-selective-classifica.tldr: The paper establishes a tight trade-off between prediction mistakes and excess abstentions when online learners receive labels only after abstaining.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization often seeks a collection of useful compromises rather than one preferred solution. The Pareto front represents solutions for which improving one objective requires sacrificing another. This paper addresses the difficulty of finding a diverse, representative collection of such solutions, particularly in high-dimensional problems.

The proposed method updates multiple candidate points in parallel. Multiple gradient descent moves those points toward the Pareto front, while a repulsive mechanism from Stein variational gradient descent encourages them to spread out. A second version uses Langevin dynamics, where diffusion noise supplies the diversity-promoting mechanism. Both versions combine progress toward good trade-offs with pressure against concentrating candidates in one region.

The authors provide theoretical convergence guarantees to the Pareto front and report more diverse, evenly distributed solutions than existing gradient-based approaches requiring predefined preference functions. Extensive experiments support the methods’ effectiveness, especially the Stein-based version. The key contribution is coordinating a population of candidate compromises so that optimization seeks both quality and coverage of the available trade-offs.
neurips-2021-profiling-pareto-front-with.tldr: Parallel gradient updates with repulsion or diffusion find diverse Pareto solutions, with theoretical convergence guarantees and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning can make good use of limited labels, but repeatedly training on a large unlabeled collection is computationally expensive. RETRIEVE asks which unlabeled examples are most useful to retain. Its central idea is that a carefully chosen subset can make existing learning algorithms converge faster and reduce their training costs.

The subset is selected through a bi-level optimization problem that combines discrete example choices with continuous model training. The selection objective is the loss on labeled data, tying the choice of unlabeled examples to the supervised task. A one-step gradient approximation makes the problem more tractable, and approximate submodularity supports using simple greedy selection algorithms.

Experiments combine RETRIEVE with VAT, Mean-Teacher, and FixMatch on several real-world datasets. The authors report around threefold training speedup in conventional semi-supervised learning with minimal accuracy degradation. Under unlabeled-data imbalance and out-of-distribution contamination, they report improved performance and a fivefold speedup relative to state-of-the-art robust methods. These results suggest that selective use of unlabeled data can improve both training efficiency and robustness in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-retrieve-coreset-selection-.tldr: RETRIEVE selects useful subsets of unlabeled data to accelerate semi-supervised training and improve robustness to imbalance and out-of-distribution data.

paragraphs: Multimodal meta-learning considers learning to adapt across several distinct kinds of tasks. Earlier work reported that a single learner trained across these modes can sometimes beat separate specialists, attributing the improvement to knowledge transfer. This paper investigates that explanation more directly by examining how individual tasks interact.

The authors introduce a task-level measure of transfer between different modes, drawing on the idea of transference from multi-task learning. This makes the analysis more detailed than comparing only overall performance of shared and specialized learners. It provides a way to quantify cross-task transfer at the level where the proposed explanation operates.

A second contribution is a new multimodal meta-learner inspired by hard parameter sharing in multi-task learning and a reinterpretation of related methods. The authors report that it outperforms existing approaches by considerable margins. Together, the analysis and model connect understanding task interactions with improving adaptation across diverse task distributions. The paper also explores how this perspective might illuminate interactions in conventional meta-learning.
neurips-2021-revisit-multimodal-meta-lea.tldr: Task-level transfer analysis and ideas from parameter sharing yield a stronger meta-learner for diverse task distributions.

paragraphs: Shift neural networks reduce computational demands by replacing expensive multiplications and representing weights with a small number of discrete values. Their appeal is faster, more energy-efficient computation. However, the paper identifies training difficulties in existing shift networks, including sensitivity to initialization, vanishing gradients, and weights whose signs become frozen.

The proposed S³ method changes how each discrete weight is represented during training. It decomposes the parameter into sign, sparsity, and shift components. This three-part representation is intended to let the low-bit weights evolve more like weights in a full-precision network. The authors report that it also makes training insensitive to weight initialization.

The stated experimental result is that three-bit shift networks can compete with full-precision counterparts on ImageNet top-1 accuracy. This matters because the motivation for shift networks depends on preserving useful predictive performance while simplifying computation. The contribution focuses on making the restricted weight representation train effectively, showing that the reported accuracy gap can be substantially addressed through the parameterization used for learning.
neurips-2021-s-3-sign-sparse-shift-repar.tldr: S³ separates sign, sparsity, and shift to train three-bit shift networks that compete with full-precision models on ImageNet accuracy.

paragraphs: Biomedical data often records which discrete events, such as genetic mutations, are present without directly showing their time evolution. This paper models those changes with continuous-time Markov chains. It shows that learning such models from the usual cross-sectional observations is generally underspecified: the observations do not fully determine the underlying temporal process.

The authors identify a potentially surprising remedy. Adding independent items to the analysis can help establish temporal order and thereby resolve underspecification. This gives a reason to retain more items, even when the common response to computational difficulty is to focus on a small collection judged most relevant.

To make that larger analysis feasible, the paper develops an approximate likelihood-maximization method that scales to hundreds of items. The authors report that it is orders of magnitude faster than previous approaches and demonstrate effectiveness on synthetic and real cancer data. The theoretical and computational contributions reinforce each other: considering additional items can help identify temporal structure, and the faster method makes that expanded modeling practical.
neurips-2021-scaling-up-continuous-time-.tldr: Including additional independent items can help identify temporal order, and a scalable Markov-chain learning method makes this strategy practical.

paragraphs: Copying a demonstrator’s actions can fail when the demonstrator has information the learner cannot observe. Different sensors, for example, can produce different information even within the same environment. Accurately modeling the learner’s visible surroundings therefore may not be enough to reproduce the demonstrator’s performance through direct behavioral imitation.

This paper extends causal imitation learning from single decisions to sequential episodes containing multiple decisions. Its central question is when successful imitation is feasible despite differences between the demonstrator’s and learner’s capabilities. The authors develop a graphical criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for this feasibility question in the studied framework.

The criterion identifies when the learner can match the demonstrator’s performance despite the information mismatch. The paper also supplies an efficient algorithm for deciding imitability and uses simulations to support the theory. This shifts attention from simply improving how closely actions are copied to determining whether the available information and causal relationships permit successful imitation across an entire sequence of decisions.
neurips-2021-sequential-causal-imitation.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion determines when sequential imitation can match a demonstrator despite differences in available information.

paragraphs: Topic models commonly represent a document through its words while setting aside dependencies among those words. This paper argues that such dependencies matter for semantic understanding and interpretability. Its Graph Neural Topic Model, or GNTM, represents each document as a directed graph whose nodes are words and whose edges encode word dependencies.

GNTM gives a probabilistic account of both the words and the graph structure. Topics include distributions over the vocabulary and over dependency edges, so they can describe relationships as well as word occurrence. A neural variational inference procedure learns the model, using graph neural networks to encode the document graphs.

The authors also establish a theoretical connection to Latent Dirichlet Allocation: LDA can be derived as a special case of GNTM with similar objective functions. This links the graph formulation to an established topic-modeling approach. Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness and interpretability relative to state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a topic representation and learning procedure that explicitly incorporates the dependencies omitted by a bag-of-words view.
neurips-2021-topic-modeling-revisited-a-.tldr: GNTM models documents as word-dependency graphs, incorporating relationships into topic learning and recovering LDA as a special case.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware, but their discrete spikes make supervised training difficult. Existing approaches often approximate derivatives or work with spike times, while propagating information through many time steps. This paper develops an alternative for networks with feedback connections by focusing on their equilibrium behavior.

The authors show that average firing rates evolve toward an equilibrium described by a fixed-point equation. They treat the forward network dynamics as a solver for that equation. Implicit differentiation then computes parameter gradients from the equilibrium relation without reversing the exact sequence of forward operations. This decouples the forward and backward procedures and avoids differentiating the discontinuous spiking functions directly.

Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, N-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate superior performance for the studied feedback models using fewer neurons and parameters and a small number of time steps. The paper also briefly discusses biological plausibility because the differentiation procedure requires another equilibrium computation. Its main contribution is an equilibrium-based route to training feedback spiking networks.
neurips-2021-training-feedback-spiking-n.tldr: Implicit differentiation of equilibrium firing rates trains feedback spiking networks without reversing their exact spike-by-spike computation.

paragraphs: TransGAN investigates whether a generative adversarial network can generate strong images using transformer architectures throughout, without convolutional layers. The design includes a generator that progressively increases feature resolution and a discriminator that examines multiple scales. These components aim to capture both broad semantic structure and fine image texture.

Scaling this design requires addressing memory demands and unstable training. The authors introduce grid self-attention to reduce the memory bottleneck and develop a training recipe using data augmentation, modified normalization, and relative position encoding. The resulting system combines architectural changes with training choices intended to make transformer-based adversarial generation practical at larger resolutions.

The paper reports state-of-the-art inception score and FID on STL-10, alongside competitive CIFAR-10 and 128-by-128 CelebA results that outperform StyleGAN-V2. At 256-by-256 resolution on CelebA-HQ and LSUN-Church, it reports diverse, high-fidelity examples with detailed textures. Visualizations of training dynamics further explore differences from convolutional generators. These findings demonstrate that the proposed transformer-only design can compete strongly in the evaluated image-generation settings.
neurips-2021-transgan-two-pure-transform.tldr: TransGAN combines transformer-only generation and discrimination with memory-saving attention and specialized training to achieve competitive image synthesis.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning is widely used to learn continuous-control behavior from demonstrations. Many proposed variations aim to improve policy performance or reduce the amount of experience required for learning. Yet these choices are rarely examined together, making it difficult to understand which algorithmic components and implementation details drive the results.

This paper builds a generic framework containing more than fifty such choices and studies their effects at large scale. The investigation includes more than half a million trained agents and uses both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. Bringing these options into one framework enables a broad empirical examination of choices that are otherwise often evaluated in separate implementations.

The authors analyze the main results and emphasize surprising findings from the study. The contribution described in the abstract is the breadth and systematic nature of this investigation, covering both high-level algorithm design and lower-level implementation decisions. It provides an empirical basis for assessing what matters in adversarial imitation learning, with attention to both learned behavior and sample efficiency.
neurips-2021-what-matters-for-adversaria.tldr: A study of over fifty design choices and half a million trained agents systematically examines what affects adversarial imitation learning.
